analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to leave a gun accessible to a child who then uses it to cause injury or death.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required adults to store guns securely in homes where a minor could get to them. It created criminal penalties—fines or up to five years in prison—but only when a child actually obtained the gun and used it to commit a crime or hurt someone. Owners who used a lock, safe, or kept the gun within arm's reach would not be liable. The bill never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families benefit if it passes: thousands of children each year are killed or injured with guns left unsecured in homes, and this makes it a federal crime when an adult's unsecured gun ends up in a child's hands and causes harm. Communities broadly benefit from fewer school and neighborhood shootings committed with guns taken from homes.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime to knowingly store a gun unsecured in a residence where a minor is likely to gain access, if a child then uses it in a crime or causes injury or death.

It exempts gun owners who keep firearms in secure storage, use a safety device like a lock, or keep the gun carried on them or within immediate reach, so the rule targets leaving loaded guns accessible to children.
Violators face up to 5 years in prison, fines, or both.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners who leave firearms accessible to minors face fines and up to five years in prison if a child uses the gun to commit a crime or causes injury or death.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners who leave guns unsecured

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new federal crime punishable by up to 5 years in prison and fines, and that penalty would fall on gun owners, potentially including a parent or relative after a child's death or crime.

The trigger is liability only after harm occurs: storing a gun unsecured with a child in the home is only prosecutable once a minor actually obtains the firearm and causes injury, death, or crime, so it does not prevent a first tragedy, only penalizes it after the fact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—fewer children shot with unsecured guns—addresses a real and preventable harm, and the bill was drawn narrowly: it penalizes only cases where a minor actually obtained the gun and used it in a crime or caused injury, and it includes exceptions for stored firearms and for guns carried or kept close at hand. The main cost is the creation of a federal crime that could apply to a grieving or negligent parent after a tragedy; how aggressively such cases would be prosecuted is uncertain. The bill contains no funding for free or subsidized lock devices, which would have made compliance easier. On balance it is a modest, targeted measure whose main weakness is enforcement design, not scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2023 and never moved, getting no hearing or vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 21, 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it stayed for the rest of the two-year Congress.
No further action was taken: no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It had 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, and was sponsored by Rep. Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat from Michigan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms industry are better off, since no federal safe-storage requirement or related penalty was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners; no federal storage law passed

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill after referral and never acted on it, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan floor fight, so the full shape of opposition is not in the record.

industries.note: The bill imposes a new federal storage requirement with criminal penalties on owners whose unsecured gun ends up in a child's hands. Gun manufacturers and dealer organizations generally opposed mandated storage rules as a step toward restricting ownership, though the bill does not regulate the manufacture or sale of firearms.
